title: AX is the only Experience that Matters - Ivan Burazin, Daytona
talk_summary: Ivan Burazin of Daytona argues that tools must be designed for autonomous agents ('agent experience'), not humans, and describes Daytona's sandbox primitives built from that principle: fast API-first sandboxes, declarative image building, shared volumes, and parallel forking.

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of an agent hand-building Docker images (brittle) or a human pre-baking them, the agent declares base image + install commands and the platform builds the image on the fly and launches a sandbox from it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: an agent can say, 'Oh, I need a net new one. This is my base image. These are the things I want installed... We build it on the fly'

takeaways.what_they_do: Large datasets are uploaded once to a volume and mounted as a network drive into every sandbox, avoiding repeated S3 download/upload per environment.

takeaways.evidence_quote: It can basically take a machine, fork it five times, 10 times, 100,000 times, go through all of these and then come to an output.

takeaways.what_they_do: Expose all key functionality via API so agents can operate without a human clicking; treat API as the underlying layer even if MCP sits on top.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the best way for an agent to interact with any tool is through a machine native interface... an API is the underlying tech that you have to have

takeaways.what_they_do: Serve clean markdown docs and an llms.txt index so agents can consume documentation without fluff.
takeaways.evidence_quote: any doc URL just appended md and you'll get a clean markdown file no fluff... if you don't have an LM llm's.txt in your docs, you definitely should.

takeaways.technique: Fast sandbox spin-up as a design constraint
takeaways.what_they_do: Optimize sandbox startup to milliseconds so interactive agents don't wait on environment provisioning.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we created something that spins up in like 27 milliseconds
